slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Disability, Rights, Identity, and Belonging
Understand disability through more than limitations, and examine the conditions that shape participation in services and work.
Foundation self-directed learning
slides.narration: Disability can be relevant to care, support, rights, identity, and community at the same time. The perspective you use influences what appears to be the problem and who is expected to change. This course compares several ways of understanding disability through public-service, employee, and engagement situations. You will consider how a description can preserve agency or obscure a barrier. The goal is a more accurate response, without deciding someone’s identity for them or substituting training for an actual service or accommodation process.

slides.text:
Who is described as the problem?
“The person cannot complete our form” directs attention toward the person.

“The form requires handwriting in small boxes” makes a design condition visible.

What could each description lead the next reader to do?
slides.narration: Both sentences might refer to the same afternoon, yet they invite different responses. The first may prompt another request that the person change how they write. The second raises a question about the document and available alternatives. The support need remains real in both accounts. A barrier-focused description does not erase it; it adds a condition staff can examine. If the first description is repeatedly reused, an unchanged design may become a recurring reason people’s participation is delayed.

slides.text:
Several perspectives answer different questions
A medical view asks about a condition or treatment. A social view asks what restricts participation in the environment.

Functional, rights-based, cultural, and intersectional views add questions about activity, entitlement, identity, and interacting barriers.

No single view describes the whole person.
slides.narration: A medical perspective can be useful when considering care and health needs. It becomes incomplete when a form or meeting design is treated as neutral and every difficulty is placed inside the person. Other perspectives ask what the activity requires, what rights apply, what disability means to the person, or how conditions interact. These questions can complement one another. The choice is not between respecting an individual need and examining a barrier. A careful account can keep both visible.

slides.text:
A program description can narrow possibility
A page describes people chiefly as unable to manage ordinary life and says staff decide what is best.

The wording may obscure strengths, chosen support, and decision-making. Repetition can normalize low expectations.

Describe the purpose and support accurately while retaining agency and any required terms.
slides.narration: Public wording helps readers understand what a program expects and offers. A description built entirely around inability may communicate that people’s own priorities have little place in the service. If reused in forms and planning conversations, that framing could influence which options staff consider. The next choice asks how to improve the account without denying support needs or changing legal terms casually. No wording change alone can establish how decisions are made in practice or whether access improves.

slides.text:
Describe support without erasing agency
A public page describes people chiefly as unable to manage life and says staff decide what is best. Which revision best improves the account without denying support needs?
A. Replace every legal or program term immediately with positive language.
B. Describe the support purpose, people’s priorities, and relevant conditions, retaining required terms for review.
C. Keep the description because people who need support cannot direct decisions.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: A program page needs to explain its purpose and relevant information accurately. The concern is that the current description treats inability as the whole person and staff preference as the main basis for decisions. Compare revisions that merely sound positive with a revision that changes the account. Required terms may need to remain, and the proper content review still matters. The person’s agency and support needs can both be visible. The fiction does not establish how any actual program operates or whether a wording change will improve people’s experience.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Replace every legal or program term immediately with positive language.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Describe the support purpose, people’s priorities, and relevant conditions, retaining required terms for review.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Keep the description because people who need support cannot direct decisions.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A positive tone cannot justify changing required terms without review. It may also conceal real needs. Describe agency and conditions accurately, then use the appropriate review; the legal wording and practical effects remain unverified.

What sentence would retain the need while making the person’s priorities visible?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Changing required terms without the appropriate review can make a description inaccurate even when the intention is respectful. Replacing difficult realities with vague positivity may also leave readers unable to understand support. The better approach preserves necessary information while examining the deficit frame. The case does not identify which terms are legally defined, and no change in actual service practice follows automatically from the rewrite.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This keeps support visible while restoring agency and context. Repeated use can challenge a deficit-only expectation. Obtain the appropriate content review and hear varied perspectives; wording alone does not prove changed practice.

What sentence would retain the need while making the person’s priorities visible?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This response describes why support exists without making need the whole identity or excluding people’s priorities. If reused, that framing may help staff consider choices that a deficit-only account misses. The proposed wording still needs appropriate review and input from relevant people. It is a supported improvement in the account, not proof that decisions, access, or outcomes have already changed.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The inference equates support with lack of agency. Repetition can narrow choices and make staff assumptions seem inevitable. Examine the person’s priorities and actual process; the description does not establish incapacity.

What sentence would retain the need while making the person’s priorities visible?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A need for support does not itself establish that someone cannot direct or influence a decision. Treating that inference as routine may narrow the options staff offer and obscure the person’s expertise. Ask about the actual decision arrangement and the person’s priorities while preserving necessary processes. The description supplies no finding about a person’s capability or the requirements of a specific service.

slides.text:
Keep health and support needs visible
Barrier removal should not erase pain, fatigue, communication needs, or other experiences a person chooses to describe.

Ask what helps with this activity rather than requesting unnecessary medical detail.

Actual care and formal processes retain their own responsibilities.
slides.narration: A social perspective makes changeable conditions visible, but it should not imply that a redesigned environment resolves every experience. Someone may need both an accessible meeting and flexibility during a health-related change. Begin with the activity and the information appropriate to your role. Do not treat a learning conversation as permission to request a diagnosis. Respect what the person offers and what remains private. A more usable process and an individual support can work together without either becoming the entire explanation.

slides.text:
Describe activity in context
A functional question asks what the person can do in a particular setting, with relevant supports.

Ability is not a fixed verdict derived from one difficult task.

Changing the tool, pace, or environment may change what becomes possible.
slides.narration: A person’s performance depends partly on the conditions of the activity. Difficulty using a mouse-only form does not establish difficulty understanding the questions. Missing information from an uncaptioned recording does not establish lack of interest in learning. Describe the activity and support conditions rather than making a broad capability judgment. This can prevent a narrow observation from becoming a repeated reason to offer fewer opportunities. What would work best still needs appropriate inquiry rather than an assumption about every person with a similar disability.

slides.text:
Rights are more than a charitable response
A rights-based view asks about access, equal opportunity, participation, and the responsibilities of the relevant process.

A helpful intention is not the same as an appropriate rights-based response.

Use the responsible agency routes for actual rights, service, or accommodation questions.
slides.narration: Considering rights changes the reason access matters. It is not only a generous extra offered when convenient; it concerns how people can participate in public life and opportunity. The precise duties depend on the setting and relevant requirements, which this introductory course does not decide. Learning can help you notice a concern and ask an informed question. It must not replace the responsible office or create an informal eligibility test. Keep actual procedures visible while considering how everyday choices support dignity and participation.

slides.text:
Disability can also be identity and culture
Disability communities include histories, languages, arts, humor, organizing, and varied views about access.

Some people understand disability as central to identity; others describe it differently.

Do not assume that a medical category tells you the person’s chosen meaning.
slides.narration: Public administration often records disability through eligibility categories. Those categories can be necessary for particular functions, yet they do not tell the whole story of a person’s life. Disability communities also hold shared knowledge and histories developed through participation and advocacy. People differ in how they understand and describe their disability. Hearing that meaning can widen a staff member’s perspective without replacing required information. Repeatedly treating disability only as deficiency may leave community expertise outside the design of services and learning.

slides.text:
Onboarding: separate the task from the default
A new employee asks for an accessible training format. A colleague treats the request as evidence the role may be unsuitable.

That inference can turn a design gap into a capability judgment before the work is examined.

Clarify the task, access barrier, and appropriate support process.
slides.narration: Onboarding is a point where early interpretations can influence later opportunity. An inaccessible learning resource may prevent someone from demonstrating knowledge, but it does not establish that the person cannot perform the role. Consider the actual task and the conditions supplied. The next case asks how to separate access from a broad judgment while retaining relevant standards. You do not know which support will be appropriate or how the employee will perform with it. Those questions require evidence beyond the request itself.

slides.text:
An access request during onboarding
A new employee requests an accessible training format. A colleague says this shows the role may not fit. What is the most useful response?
A. Clarify the task and format barrier, then use the appropriate access process without assuming capability.
B. Reduce future assignments because the employee has already shown a limitation.
C. Promise every requested change without examining the task or relevant process.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The training format and the role’s actual work are related but not identical. A person may understand the subject while being unable to use the version supplied. The early inference could shape assignments or development before that distinction is examined. Consider a response that preserves appropriate standards and responsibilities while making access possible to assess. Neither lowering expectations automatically nor promising everything provides that inquiry. The fiction does not identify a diagnosis, a final accommodation, or the employee’s eventual performance, and none is needed for this learning choice.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Clarify the task and format barrier, then use the appropriate access process without assuming capability.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Reduce future assignments because the employee has already shown a limitation.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Promise every requested change without examining the task or relevant process.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This separates the access condition from a broad ability judgment. It may interrupt a repeated gate to development. Clarify appropriate support and assess relevant work fairly; performance with that support is still unknown.

What does the access request tell you, and what does it not establish?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The response makes the unavailable format a condition to examine rather than a verdict about the employee. That can keep a development route open while the appropriate process considers support. The actual task and relevant standards still matter. You do not yet know what arrangement will work or how the employee will perform with it. Those questions should remain open instead of being answered by the request alone.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The inference turns an unavailable format into a capability verdict. Repetition can restrict development before work is considered. Examine the task and access route; the request does not establish unsuitability.

What does the access request tell you, and what does it not establish?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Restricting assignments based on the request makes access difficulty into presumed inability. If repeated, employees facing inaccessible onboarding resources may receive fewer opportunities to demonstrate or develop expertise. Examine the format, task, and relevant access route instead. The case establishes a request and a colleague’s inference; it does not establish capability, unsuitability, or a later employment result.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
An unlimited promise can create inaccurate expectations and bypass relevant responsibilities. Consider the task and appropriate process. A supported response is possible without presuming every request or outcome is settled.

What does the access request tell you, and what does it not establish?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A promise without examining the task can disregard legitimate requirements and the responsible process. It may leave the employee expecting a change no one has authority to provide. A supportive response clarifies the barrier and connects with the appropriate route while keeping expectations accurate. The need deserves attention, but the case does not settle the specific arrangement or guarantee its effectiveness.

slides.text:
Language preferences belong to people
Person-first and identity-first language can each be meaningful in different contexts.

Ask and follow a person’s preference when appropriate; do not impose one universal rule.

Required legal wording and general public writing may need different review.
slides.narration: Someone may prefer “disabled person,” while someone else prefers “person with a disability.” The preference can reflect identity, history, or simply what feels respectful to them. You cannot infer it reliably from a broad category. In public materials, use informed, clear wording and the appropriate review process, especially when terms are defined in law or rule. Changing a label without changing the underlying description may still leave a deficit frame intact. Consider both the words and the agency they communicate.

slides.text:
Belonging includes opportunity to contribute
Welcoming language matters, but participation also depends on usable arrangements and recognition of expertise.

Consider access to assignments, learning, feedback, and advancement where relevant.

A friendly interaction does not establish that the whole employee experience is accessible.
slides.narration: An employee can feel welcomed by colleagues and still encounter a training or assignment route they cannot use. Examine the opportunity involved rather than treating goodwill as proof of access. A recurring design or credibility assumption may affect development later in employment. That is a mechanism to investigate, not a judgment about every supervisor or outcome. Ask what makes the activity usable and how contribution is recognized. The employee’s chosen account and actual criteria help distinguish a specific barrier from a broad impression.

slides.text:
Interdependence can support self-direction
People commonly rely on relationships, tools, and shared knowledge to pursue their goals.

Using support does not automatically remove agency or make a person’s priorities less important.

Ask how the person wants support involved rather than equating independence with doing everything alone.
slides.narration: Much of ordinary life involves interdependence, including asking colleagues for expertise or using technology to complete a task. Disability perspectives can make those relationships more visible. A person may direct a choice while relying on support to understand or communicate it. The arrangement should be examined in context through the appropriate process, not assumed from a diagnosis. If support is routinely treated as incapacity, people’s preferences may become less visible. A better question asks what helps the person pursue the goal they identify.

slides.text:
Learn with self-advocates and varied communities
Community briefs can prepare questions about history, access, and institutional experience.

Self-advocates bring expertise that a description of needs alone may miss.

Invite varied, voluntary perspectives without assigning representation by disability or other identity.
slides.narration: The people affected by a service have knowledge about how it works in their lives. That expertise can inform a description, invitation, or process while remaining different from legal or program responsibilities. A community brief can help staff prepare but cannot establish a person’s preference or speak for every disability community. Invite participation through usable routes and explain its possible influence. Repeatedly consulting only familiar voices may miss other experiences. Learning should make room for that variation without turning anyone into a representative by default.

slides.text:
Do not reduce engagement to a personal story
A planning group asks one disabled participant to share an inspiring story rather than comment on the service design.

The request can replace practical expertise with a familiar narrative and leave the design question unanswered.

Invite the person’s chosen contribution to an open question.
slides.narration: A personal story can be valuable when freely offered, but it should not be the price of being heard. The participant may have useful knowledge about a form, schedule, or decision route. Asking only for inspiration can cast them as a symbol while staff keep the practical analysis to themselves. If repeated, engagement may collect stories without changing the conditions people identify. The next choice asks how to welcome expertise without requiring disclosure or assuming the participant represents all disabled people.

slides.text:
Invite expertise rather than an inspiration story
At a service-design session, a disabled participant is asked to share an inspiring personal story instead of commenting on the form under review. Which invitation is better?
A. Ask them to represent every disabled person’s needs.
B. Remove the participant from the review because lived experience is not technical expertise.
C. Invite their chosen observations about the form, with usable participation and no required personal disclosure.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: Personal experience can be a valuable contribution, but it need not be presented as an inspiring story to earn attention. The participant may know how a form works in practice and which assumptions it makes. Your invitation should leave room for that expertise and for the person to choose what they share. A culture brief may prepare staff for relevant questions without replacing the account. Consider what each option does to agency and to the practical review. The person’s willingness, views, and the eventual design decision are not supplied.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Ask them to represent every disabled person’s needs.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Remove the participant from the review because lived experience is not technical expertise.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Invite their chosen observations about the form, with usable participation and no required personal disclosure.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Representation by identity can burden one person and turn a narrow account into a universal claim. Invite their chosen perspective and hear varied voices; the wider community’s views are unknown.

What question would let the person influence the form without requiring a biography?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A person can hold useful knowledge without being a representative for every disability experience. Assigning that role may pressure disclosure and allow staff to treat one account as everyone’s preference. If repeated, other perspectives remain missing. Ask about the particular form and invite the person’s chosen contribution through usable arrangements. The wider range of views and the person’s willingness to participate remain unknown.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Excluding lived experience may leave a usability barrier invisible. Repeating that boundary can keep design assumptions untested. Invite relevant observations alongside other expertise; the participant’s specific contribution is not yet known.

What question would let the person influence the form without requiring a biography?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Technical knowledge and lived experience answer different questions and can inform one another. Removing the participant may leave staff unable to see a practical access condition the form creates. Repeating that exclusion keeps the design based on insider assumptions. Invite relevant feedback while preserving the appropriate decision process. The case does not establish that every observation will warrant a change or that participation guarantees a usable result.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This recognizes practical expertise and preserves choice. It can interrupt a routine that collects stories while leaving design questions to insiders. Explain possible influence and hear varied accounts; participation and improvements remain open.

What question would let the person influence the form without requiring a biography?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: The invitation connects the participant’s expertise with an actual open question while preserving choice about disclosure. It may help the review examine a condition that an inspiration narrative would leave untouched. Explain what the input can influence and seek other relevant perspectives. The contribution is invited, not already given, and the fiction does not supply a revised form or a verified improvement in experience.

slides.text:
A deficit frame can travel into decisions
A broad description of inability may be copied into notes, templates, and planning assumptions.

Future readers may offer fewer choices without examining the original conditions.

Keep the account specific and identify the barrier that could be reviewed.
slides.narration: Written descriptions can outlast the situation that produced them. “Unable to participate” may later be treated as a fixed fact, even if the original problem concerned a particular format. A narrower description helps future readers ask the right question. It also leaves room for changed circumstances and the person’s own priorities. Examine how the wording is reused and where an appropriate correction belongs. This identifies a possible repeated mechanism; it does not establish that every later decision was caused by one sentence.

slides.text:
Support today and design for the next person
An immediate alternative can help with the present task. A design review can reduce the need to request the same workaround repeatedly.

Neither response guarantees every access need is met.

Ask whether the person can use the actual arrangement and what remains difficult.
slides.narration: Some barriers need a practical response now while a broader change takes time. The immediate support and the design review can complement one another. Do not leave someone waiting for a perfect redesign when an appropriate alternative is available, or declare the system solved because one person found a workaround. A recurring burden to ask again may still matter. Listen through the relevant channels and examine the actual activity. A useful adjustment can be recognized while uncertainty about wider effectiveness remains.

slides.text:
Rewrite a description without losing the need
Use the form, program description, or training example.

Retain the relevant support need, restore the person’s agency, and name a changeable condition.

What would a later reader understand differently? No personal record is needed.
slides.narration: Try changing the explanation rather than simply replacing a word. Instead of “cannot learn the material,” you might describe the unavailable format and what remains unknown about understanding. Instead of “staff decide what is best,” describe how the person’s priorities inform support within the actual process. Keep necessary terms and responsibilities intact. Your reflection can remain private. The test is whether the revised account makes both the person and the surrounding condition more accurately visible to someone reading it later.

slides.text:
A new perspective is not a completed finding
Recognizing a barrier or reframing a sentence is a meaningful learning step.

An approved change, usable support, and improved experience each need their own evidence.

Missing feedback leaves a question open; it does not establish success or failure.
slides.narration: Learning can change what you notice before any formal action occurs. That matters, yet it should not be described as an approved accommodation or an improved service outcome. Keep the stages distinct: understanding, a proposed response, an actual change, and information about its effect. The relevant office retains its decisions. A person’s silence does not prove acceptance or remove the concern. Honest limits support a more useful follow-through because they show what is known and what still needs attention.

slides.text:
Keep the whole person in view
Disability perspectives can reveal support needs, rights, identity, expertise, and environmental barriers together.

Use the lens that clarifies the question without turning it into a complete description of someone.

Continue with accessibility, person-centered thinking, and community engagement when useful.
slides.narration: The central lesson is not that one perspective always wins. It is that an incomplete perspective can narrow the response and hide a condition that staff could examine. Medical and functional questions can remain relevant alongside rights, identity, and environmental access. Hear the person’s own account and keep required responsibilities clear. The practice cases show how words and routines can influence possibilities over time. A more accurate description is a beginning that invites appropriate action and continued learning without presuming every result.

outcomes: Compare medical, social, cultural, and rights-based ways of understanding disability.
Recognize how a deficit description can obscure a person’s strengths and the surrounding barriers.
Distinguish an individual support need from a condition the organization can change.
Respect disability identity without expecting any person to represent all disabled people.
